title: Nominal vs. Verbal Sentences
subtitle: Master the difference between sentences starting with a noun versus a verb
keyPoint: In Arabic, sentences that start with a noun are nominal (equational in the present tense with no 'is/are' verb), whereas sentences starting with a verb are verbal and conventionally place the verb before the subject.

mistakes.note: Arabic does not use a present tense 'to be' verb (like يكون) to join a subject and predicate in simple present nominal sentences.
When a verb begins a verbal sentence (VSO), it remains singular even if the following subject is plural.
Be sure you place the subject in nominative case (damma) and establish a clear topic-predicate relationship without dropping essential parts.

quiz.question: Choose the correct nominal sentence meaning 'The city is wide':
quiz.explanation: A nominal sentence connects the definite subject (المدينةُ) to an indefinite predicate (واسعةٌ) without any present tense auxiliary verb.

quiz.question: Choose the correct verbal sentence meaning 'The students (m.) wrote the homework':
quiz.explanation: In classical VSO verbal order, the verb precedes the subject and must stay singular (كتبَ, not كتبوا), agreeing only in masculine gender with الطلاب.

quiz.question: Complete the nominal sentence: 'The university ___'
quiz.explanation: الجامعة (the university) is feminine singular, so its predicate adjective must be feminine singular and nominative (جديدةٌ).

quiz.question: Identify which of the following is a proper Jumla Fi'liyya (Verbal Sentence):
quiz.explanation: A Jumla Fi'liyya begins with a verb. 'أكل الطفل التفاحة' starts directly with the past tense verb أكل.

tip: To determine the sentence type, look strictly at the first word: starting with an Ism (noun/pronoun) makes it nominal; starting with a Fi'l (verb) makes it verbal.

title: Sun and Moon Letters
subtitle: Pronounce the definite article 'al-' with smooth phonetic assimilation
keyPoint: When attaching the definite article 'al-' (الـ), pronounce the 'L' clearly before the 14 Moon letters, but assimilate the 'L' completely into the 14 coronal Sun letters by doubling them with a shaddah.

cells: Clear articulation: L is fully pronounced
t, th, d, dh, r, z, s, sh, s, d, t, z, l, n
Memorized via phrase: ابغِ حَجَّكَ وَخَفْ عَقِيمَهُ

mistakes.note: Do not voice the 'L' before sun letters like sheen; assimilate into the consonant and mark with a shaddah.
The definite article consists of an alif followed by lam; never place a hamza underneath or on top of the lam itself.

mistakes.wrong: الـ كتاب جديد (separating 'al' with a space)
mistakes.note: The article 'al-' is a proclitic particle and must be attached directly to the noun without any intervening space.

quiz.question: Which of the following words begins with a Sun letter?
quiz.explanation: The letter Sheen (ش) is a Sun letter; the 'L' assimilates, yielding 'ash-shaari' '.

quiz.question: Which of the following words begins with a Moon letter?
quiz.explanation: Kaf (ك) is a Moon letter; the 'L' is articulated explicitly as 'al-kitaab'.

quiz.question: What happens to the letter Ta (ت) when the article الـ is attached to تفاح?
options: The 'L' is silent and Ta takes a sukoon.
The 'L' is dropped from the written script completely.
The 'L' assimilates and Ta takes a shaddah: التُّفَّاح.
quiz.explanation: Ta is a coronal Sun letter, so the 'L' assimilates phonetically into 'at-' and the Ta receives a shaddah (التُّفاح).

quiz.question: Identify the word containing a Moon letter among these options:
quiz.explanation: Jeem (ج) is classified as a Moon letter in standard Arabic (al-jaami'ah), while thaa, daal, and noon are Sun letters.

tip: All Sun letters are articulated along the front teeth, ridge, and tongue tip (coronal sounds); your tongue naturally wants to stay at the front rather than jump back to pronounce the 'L'.

title: Gender and Adjective Agreement
subtitle: Distinguish masculine from feminine and match descriptive adjectives perfectly
keyPoint: Every Arabic noun is masculine or feminine; adjectives follow their noun in gender, definiteness, and case.

cells: Adjective adds ة to match feminine noun
Both noun and adjective take الـ
Both noun and adjective take الـ

useCases.label: Describing Natural Gender
useCases.example: هَذَا وَلَدٌ ذَكِيٌّ وَهَذِهِ بِنْتٌ ذَكِيَّةٌ.

mistakes.note: Because سيارة ends with Ta Marbuta (feminine), the descriptive adjective must also take Ta Marbuta (جديدة).
Female beings (بنت, أم) are inherently feminine; their descriptors and predicates must be feminine.
بَيْت is grammatically masculine (ending in an open 'taa', not Ta Marbuta), so its adjective must remain masculine.

quiz.question: Select the correct phrase for 'a beautiful garden':
quiz.explanation: حَدِيقَةٌ is feminine and indefinite (tanween); its matching adjective must be feminine and indefinite (جَمِيلَةٌ).

quiz.question: Select the correct phrase for 'the small boy':
quiz.explanation: For an attributive phrase ('the small boy'), both the noun and adjective must agree in definiteness (both take الـ) and masculine gender.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'الغُرْفَةُ ___'
quiz.explanation: الغرفة is feminine; therefore, the predicate adjective must be feminine and nominative (نَظِيفَةٌ).

quiz.question: Which of the following is inherently feminine despite lacking a Ta Marbuta?
quiz.explanation: أم (mother) is feminine by biological gender/meaning, so it takes feminine agreement (أُمٌّ كَرِيمَةٌ).

tip: An Arabic adjective comes AFTER the noun it modifies, acting like a mirror: whatever definiteness, gender, or case marker the noun has, the adjective reflects.

title: The Genitive Construct (Idafa)
subtitle: Express ownership, association, and compound concepts without prepositions
keyPoint: An Idafa links two nouns (Noun 1 of Noun 2); the first noun (mudaf) never takes 'al-' or tanween, while the second noun (mudaf ilayh) sits in the genitive case (kasra).

cells: No الـ, NO Tanween, takes case by position
Last term indefinite -> whole phrase indefinite

mistakes.note: The first noun (mudaf) can NEVER take the definite article 'al-'.
The first noun (mudaf) loses its tanween when placed into an annexation phrase.
Native Arabic prefers direct annexation (Idafa) over using the preposition 'min' for possession and relationship.

quiz.question: How do you correctly say 'the doctor's car' in Arabic?
quiz.explanation: The first word cannot have 'al-' or tanween (سَيَّارَةُ), and the second word takes 'al-' with genitive kasra (الطَّبِيبِ).

quiz.question: Why is 'الكَلْبُ الحَارِسِ' ungrammatical as an Idafa?
options: Because the second word has a kasra.
Because the first word has the definite article 'al-'.
quiz.explanation: The mudaf (first term) is strictly prohibited from carrying the definite article 'al-'.

quiz.question: Choose the phrase meaning 'the door of a house' (indefinite house):
quiz.explanation: To make an entire Idafa indefinite, leave the final noun without 'al-' but with genitive tanween kasr (بَابُ بَيْتٍ).

quiz.question: In the phrase 'مَفَاتِيحُ الغُرْفَةِ ضَائِعَةٌ', what case ending belongs on 'الغُرْفَة'?
quiz.explanation: The second term of an Idafa (mudaf ilayh) is always in the genitive case, marked by a kasra (الغرفةِ).

tip: Think of the first noun in an Idafa as already 'specified' by the second noun: adding 'al-' or tanween to it would create redundant double-marking.

title: Attached Pronouns (Dama'ir Muttasila)
subtitle: Use suffix pronouns to show possession, prepositional targets, and verbal objects
keyPoint: Attached pronouns are suffixes added directly to nouns to signify possession ('my', 'your', 'his'), to prepositions, or to verbs to serve as direct objects.

mistakes.note: Independent subject pronouns like أنا cannot be placed next to a noun for possession; use the attached suffix ـي.
A noun with an attached possessive suffix is already definite; never prefix 'al-' (الكتابي is incorrect).
When attaching a pronoun to a noun ending in Ta Marbuta (ـة), the Ta Marbuta converts into an open 'T' sound and letter (ت).

quiz.question: How do you write 'her pen' in Arabic?
quiz.explanation: The attached suffix for the 3rd person feminine singular ('her') is ـهَا (qalamuhā).

quiz.question: What is the attached pronoun in the word 'سَأَلُونَا' (they asked us)?
quiz.explanation: ـنَا (-nā) is the 1st person plural attached object pronoun meaning 'us'.

quiz.question: What happens to the Ta Marbuta of 'مَدْرَسَة' when adding 'your (masc.)' (ـكَ)?
options: It stays as ة with sukoon: مَدْرَسَةْكَ.
It turns into an open pronounced Ta (ت): مَدْرَسَتُكَ.
It transforms into an alif: مَدْرَسَاكَ.
quiz.explanation: A Ta Marbuta always uncurls into an audible regular 'taa' (ت) when followed by any attached pronoun suffix.

quiz.question: Select the correct combination for 'with him' using the preposition مَعَ:
quiz.explanation: The 3rd person masculine attached suffix is ـهُ, producing مَعَهُ ('ma'ahu' - with him).

tip: Remember: attached pronouns turn a noun into an Idafa construct. That is why a noun with a possessive suffix can never have 'al-' (الـ) in front of it.

title: Past Tense Suffix Conjugation
subtitle: Conjugate regular Form I verbs in the past tense using standard suffix endings
keyPoint: In Arabic, the past tense is formed entirely by attaching personal pronoun suffixes to the three-letter verb root.

mistakes.note: Do not leave the verb in the dictionary base form (he-form) when the subject is 'I'; attach the suffix -tu.
A feminine singular subject in the past tense requires the feminine marker suffix -at (ـَتْ).
Use the masculine plural suffix -uu (ـوا) for masculine plural groups, not the feminine plural -na.

quiz.question: Choose the correct past verb for: 'Yesterday, I ___ Arabic.'
quiz.explanation: The first-person singular suffix ('I') in the past tense is -tu (ـتُ), giving دَرَسْتُ.

quiz.question: Choose the correct past verb for: 'Fatima ___ coffee.'
quiz.explanation: Fatima is third-person feminine singular (she), which requires the suffix -at (ـَتْ), yielding شَرِبَتْ.

quiz.question: Choose the correct past verb for: 'We ___ to the market.'
quiz.explanation: The first-person plural suffix ('we') is -naa (ـنا), producing ذَهَبْنا.

quiz.question: Choose the correct past verb for: 'The students (m.pl.) ___ the lesson.'
quiz.explanation: Third-person masculine plural requires the suffix -uu (ـوا) with a silent alif, forming فَهِمُوا.

tip: The 3rd-person masculine singular form (e.g. كَتَبَ) carries no extra suffix and serves as the primary base entry in Arabic dictionaries.

title: Present Tense Prefix/Suffix Conjugation
subtitle: Conjugate imperfective verbs for habitual and ongoing actions using person markers
keyPoint: Present tense verbs in Arabic require a person-marking prefix (أ / ت / ي / ن), sometimes accompanied by a suffix to denote gender or plurality.

mistakes.note: Use prefix alif (أَ) for 'I' (أنا), not the prefix yaa (يَ), which marks 'he'.
Addressing a female singular (أنتِ) requires both the prefix ta- and suffix -iina (تَـ...ـِينَ).
When the plural subject precedes the verb, the verb must show full plural agreement with -uuna (ـُونَ).

quiz.question: Select the correct verb: 'Every morning, I ___ milk.'
quiz.explanation: First-person singular takes the prefix hamza/alif (أَ), resulting in أَشْرَبُ.

quiz.question: Select the correct verb: 'Where do you (female singular) ___?'
quiz.explanation: Second-person feminine singular (أنتِ) takes prefix ta- and suffix -iina, forming تَسْكُنِينَ.

quiz.question: Select the correct verb: 'We ___ new vocabulary.'
quiz.explanation: First-person plural ('we') always uses prefix nuun (نَ), making نَحْفَظُ.

quiz.question: Select the correct verb: 'The engineers (m.pl.) ___ the project.'
quiz.explanation: Third-person masculine plural takes prefix ya- and suffix -uuna (يَـ...ـُونَ), giving يَعْمَلُونَ.

tip: Notice that تَكْتُبُ can mean both 'you (m.sg.) write' and 'she writes'; sentence context and subject pronouns will clarify which one is intended.

title: Broken Plurals (Jam' Taksir)
subtitle: Form plurals by shifting internal vowel patterns instead of attaching standard suffixes
keyPoint: The majority of masculine and non-human Arabic nouns form plurals by altering their internal vowel template rather than adding standard end suffixes.

mistakes.note: Do not attach the regular sound plural ending -uun to inanimate nouns like kitaab; use its broken plural kutub.
The plural of qalam (pen) is aqlaam (أقلام), not regular feminine plural -aat.
The word rajul (man) forms a broken plural rijaal (رجال), never sound masculine *rajuluun.

quiz.question: What is the broken plural form of بَيْت (house)?
quiz.explanation: بَيْت follows the pattern فُعُول (fu'uul) to become بُيُوت.

quiz.question: What is the broken plural of وَلَد (boy)?
quiz.explanation: وَلَد follows the أَفْعال (af'aal) pattern to form أَوْلاد.

quiz.question: What is the correct broken plural of مَدْرَسَة (school)?
quiz.explanation: مَدْرَسَة takes the broken plural pattern مَفاعِل (mafaa'il), becoming مَدارِس.

quiz.question: What is the broken plural of مَدينَة (city)?
quiz.explanation: The standard broken plural for مَدينَة in modern Arabic is مُدُن (mudun).

tip: Whenever you memorize a new singular Arabic noun, always memorize its broken plural alongside it like a single vocabulary pair.

title: The Non-Human Plural Rule
subtitle: Treat plural non-human nouns as grammatically feminine singular for all agreement
keyPoint: All non-human plural nouns (animals, objects, ideas) require feminine singular adjectives, pronouns, demonstratives, and verbs.

mistakes.note: هَؤُلاءِ is only used for human plurals; non-human plurals must use the feminine singular demonstrative هَذِهِ.
Non-human plurals cannot take masculine sound plural adjectives; they take feminine singular (كَبِيرَة).
Verbs referring back to non-human plurals must be inflected in the feminine singular form (جَرَتْ).

quiz.question: Fill in the blank: '___ are ancient cities.'
quiz.explanation: مُدُن (cities) is a non-human plural, so it requires the feminine singular demonstrative هَذِهِ.

quiz.question: Choose the correct adjective: 'I bought new pens: اشْتَرَيْتُ أَقْلاماً ___.'
quiz.explanation: أقلام is a non-human plural noun; its modifying adjective must be feminine singular (جَديدَةً).

quiz.question: Choose the correct verb: 'The cars ___ fast.'
quiz.explanation: Plural non-human subjects take a 3rd-person feminine singular verb (تَسِيرُ).

quiz.question: Choose the correct pronoun: 'I found the keys and took ___ (them).'
quiz.explanation: Keys (مَفاتِيح) are non-human plural, referring to them requires the feminine singular pronoun suffix ـها.

tip: Memorize the classic golden rule of Arabic syntax: 'Every non-human plural is feminine singular' (كُلُّ جَمْعٍ لا يَعْقِلُ مُؤَنَّثٌ).

title: The Dual (Al-Muthanna) in Nouns and Verbs
subtitle: Inflect words for exactly two entities using dedicated dual endings
keyPoint: Arabic has a distinct grammatical dual number marked by -aan/-ayn on nouns and -aa on verbs to represent exactly two people or items.

mistakes.note: Do not use the numeral two followed by a singular noun in Arabic; decline the noun itself directly into the dual (كِتابانِ).
In the accusative object position, the dual takes suffix -ayn (ـَيْنِ), not nominative -aan (ـانِ).
Verbs agreeing with two subjects must take the dual verb suffix alif (ـا), not the plural suffix (ـوا).

quiz.question: Fill in the blank with the subject: 'The two students (m.) arrived: وَصَلَ ___.'
quiz.explanation: As the subject (nominative / marfoo'), the dual noun requires the ending -aan (ـانِ), giving الطّالِبانِ.

quiz.question: Choose the correct verb: 'The two girls ___ the lesson.'
quiz.explanation: For two females in the past tense, the verb takes the feminine dual suffix -ataa (ـتا), yielding فَهِمَتا.

quiz.question: Fill in the blank: 'I ate at two restaurants: أَكَلْتُ في ___.'
quiz.explanation: Following the preposition في (genitive / majroor), the dual noun takes the suffix -ayn (ـَيْنِ): مَطْعَمَيْنِ.

quiz.question: Choose the correct present tense verb: 'The two brothers ___ every morning.'
quiz.explanation: Third-person masculine dual in the present tense adds the dual ending -aani (ـانِ), producing يَتَكَلَّمانِ.

tip: Distinguish between the dual suffix -ayn (ـَيْنِ, with fat-ha before yaa) and the sound masculine plural -iin (ـِينَ, with kasra before yaa).

title: Core Negation (Maa, Laa, Laysa)
subtitle: Master the primary tools for negating past, present, and equational sentences
keyPoint: Use maa to negate past actions, laa for present habits, and laysa to negate equational nominal sentences.

useCases.label: Habitual Present
useCases.example: أَنَا لا آكُلُ اللَّحْمَ فِي الصَّبَاحِ.

examples.en: نَحْنُ لَسْنَا طُلاَّبًا فِي هَذِهِ الجَامِعَةِ.

mistakes.note: Use 'maa' (or 'lam' + jussive) to negate past actions; 'laa' is reserved for present or imperative contexts.
To negate an active present-tense verb directly, use 'laa' instead of 'laysa'.
The predicate of 'laysa' (khabar laysa) must be placed in the accusative case with nasb (fathatayn).

quiz.question: Yesterday, Fatima ___ her homework.
quiz.explanation: Negating a past tense verb requires 'maa' directly preceding the verb.

quiz.question: He ___ milk at all.
quiz.explanation: Regular present habitual actions are negated using 'laa'.

quiz.question: The exam is ___ difficult.
quiz.explanation: 'Laysa' negates nominal sentences, and its predicate takes the accusative marker (-an).

quiz.question: We ___ ready for the test.
quiz.explanation: 'Laysa' conjugates like a past verb: 'lasnaa' matches the first person plural 'we'.

tip: Remember that 'laysa' conjugates as a past-tense verb in form, but strictly refers to present-tense states.

title: Derived Verb Forms II, III, and IV
subtitle: Augment root verbs to express causation, interaction, and direct transitivity
keyPoint: Derive Form II by doubling the middle radical (fa''ala), Form III by lengthening the first vowel (faa'ala), and Form IV by prefixing a hamza (af'ala).

mistakes.note: Form I 'alima' means 'to know'; to express 'to teach' (causing someone to know), Form II 'allama' is needed.
Use Form III 'kaataba' to express mutual correspondence without needing unnecessary prepositional clutter.
'Kharaja' is intransitive ('he exited'); to make it transitive ('he took out'), Form IV 'akhraja' must be used.

quiz.question: Which verb form pattern represents Form II?
quiz.explanation: Form II is characterized by doubling the second root radical with a shaddah: fa''ala.

quiz.question: To express mutual helping or assisting someone, use:
quiz.explanation: Form III 'faa'ala' often conveys an action directed at another person, such as 'saa'ada' (to assist).

quiz.question: The verb أَرْسَلَ belongs to which derived form?
quiz.explanation: Form IV follows the pattern 'af'ala' with an initial hamza and sukun on the first radical.

quiz.question: The present tense prefix for Forms II, III, and IV always takes which vowel?
quiz.explanation: Forms II, III, and IV are unique in having a dammah on their present-tense prefix (yu-fa''ilu, yu-faa'ilu, yu-f'ilu).

tip: Check the present-tense prefix: if it carries a dammah ('yu-'), the verb is almost certainly Form II, III, or IV.

title: The Three Grammatical Cases (I'rab: Raf', Nasb, Jarr)
subtitle: Track subjects, objects, and possessives through standard case declensions
keyPoint: Arabic nouns decline into three cases: raf' (nominative for subjects), nasb (accusative for objects), and jarr (genitive for prepositions and possession).

mistakes.note: The direct object of a verb must take nasb with a fat-hah ('at-taaliba'), not raf'.
In an idafa, the head noun takes its regular role marker, while the mudaf ilayh is strictly genitive (jarr).
Any noun preceded by a preposition like 'ila' must be in the genitive case marked by kasrah.

quiz.question: Identify the case of the underlined subject: 'نَامَ الطِّفْلُ'
quiz.explanation: The doer of an action (faa'il) is in the nominative case, known as marfoo'.

quiz.question: Complete with the correct direct object: 'اشْتَرَى وَالِدِي ___'
quiz.explanation: Direct objects take nasb, which for indefinite singular nouns is marked by fathatayn (-an).

quiz.question: Complete the idafa: 'مِفْتَاحُ ___ عَلَى الطَّاوِلَةِ'
quiz.explanation: The second term of a possessive construct (al-mudaaf ilayh) is always in jarr with a kasrah.

quiz.question: Dual nouns take the suffix '-ayni' in which two cases?
quiz.explanation: Dual nouns take '-aani' in raf', and change to '-ayni' in both nasb and jarr.

tip: Remember that prepositions and possessive constructs (idafa) are the ONLY two triggers that cause a noun to take jarr.

title: Subjunctive and Jussive Moods (Al-Mansub wa Al-Majzum)
subtitle: Alter present verb endings to signal intent, strict negation, and commands
keyPoint: Particles like 'an' and 'lan' place the imperfect verb into the subjunctive (mansub, ending in -a), while 'lam' and 'laa' al-naahiya place it into the jussive (majzum, ending in sukun).

mistakes.note: The complementizer 'an' triggers the subjunctive mood, changing the final vowel from dammah to fat-hah.
The past-negator particle 'lam' triggers the jussive mood, replacing dammah with a sukun.
'Lan' cannot precede past-tense verbs; it strictly governs imperfect subjunctive verbs to negate future actions.

quiz.question: Which particle negates future actions and triggers the subjunctive?
quiz.explanation: 'Lan' indicates emphatic future negation and requires the subjunctive verb form ending in fat-hah.

quiz.question: Choose the correct ending: 'يَجِبُ عَلَيْكَ أَنْ ___'
quiz.explanation: Following the subjunctive particle 'an', the singular masculine imperfect takes fat-hah.

quiz.question: The particle 'لَمْ' conveys past negation and triggers which mood?
quiz.explanation: 'Lam' is one of the primary particles of jazm (jussive), negating past action using the present tense stem.

quiz.question: In plural verbs ending in '-oona', what happens in subjunctive and jussive moods?
options: The noon turns into a meem
A fat-hah is added after noon
quiz.explanation: Verbs of the 'Five Verbs' paradigm (like yaktuboona) drop the final noon (hazf an-noon) in both nasb and jazm.

tip: Pairings to memorize: 'an/lan' always take fat-hah (subjunctive), while 'lam/laa' prohibition always take sukun (jussive).

title: Derived Verb Forms V through X
subtitle: Uncover subtle semantic layers: reflexives, reciprocity, and seeking states
keyPoint: Higher verb forms build upon lower roots to systematically express reflexivity (Forms V & VIII), cooperation (Form VI), passivity (Form VII), and requests (Form X).

examples.en: اِشْتَغَلَ العُمَّالُ فِي المَصْنَعِ طَوَالَ اليَوْمِ.

mistakes.note: 'Kasara' means someone broke something; use Form VII 'inkasara' when an object breaks by itself without an agent.
Rather than using reflexive pronouns, Arabic employs Form V 'ta'allama' to express learning (teaching oneself).
Form X 'istaghfara' inherently contains the meaning 'to seek forgiveness', making additional nouns redundant.

quiz.question: Form X verbs ('istaf'ala') predominantly signify:
quiz.explanation: The prefix 'ista-' frequently denotes asking for, requesting, or estimating the root concept (e.g. istakhdama, istaghfara).

quiz.question: Which verb demonstrates the reciprocal Form VI pattern?
quiz.explanation: 'Ta'aawana' follows the 'tafaa'ala' pattern representing reciprocal cooperation among multiple participants.

quiz.question: The verb 'اِنْقَطَعَ' (to be cut off) is which derived form?
quiz.explanation: Verbs beginning with an unvocalized alif followed by noon (infa'ala) are Form VII, denoting intransitive or reflexive passivity.

quiz.question: What is the primary structural difference between Form II and Form V?
quiz.explanation: Form V (tafa''ala) is formed by adding the prefix 'ta-' to the doubled middle radical of Form II (fa''ala).

tip: Whenever you spot the prefix 'ista-' (اِسْتَـ), assume the verb means 'to seek' or 'to request' whatever root concept follows.

title: Kana and Its Sisters (Kana wa Akhawatuha)
subtitle: Expressing past, ongoing, or transformed states by marking the predicate accusative
keyPoint: Verbs in this family leave the subject in the nominative (Marfu') but shift the predicate into the accusative (Mansub).

cells: Accusative predicate marked with Tanwin Fatha
Accusative predicate showing change of state

examples.en: ما زالَ الوَلَدُ نائِماً في غُرْفَتِهِ.

mistakes.note: The predicate of kana must be in the accusative (Mansub) with fatha/tanwin fatha, never nominative (damma).
Kana and its sisters must agree in gender with their subject; add the feminine ta (ت) for feminine subjects.
Dual predicates take the accusative dual ending -ayn (ـَيْنِ) instead of the nominative -an (ـانِ).

quiz.question: Choose the correct predicate: 'كانَ البابُ ___.' (The door was open)
quiz.explanation: The predicate of kana takes the accusative case, marked here by tanwin fatha (مَفْتوحاً).

quiz.question: Fill in the blank: '___ الحَقيقَةُ واضِحَةً.' (The truth became clear)
quiz.explanation: The subject 'الحَقيقَةُ' is grammatically feminine, so the verb must take the feminine suffix 'صارَتْ'.

quiz.question: Select the correct form for plural: 'كانَ المُهَنْدِسونَ ___.' (The engineers were hardworking)
quiz.explanation: Sound masculine plurals take -ina (ـينَ) in the accusative case as the predicate of kana.

quiz.question: Complete the negation: 'لَيْسَ الكِتابُ ___.' (The book is not useful)
quiz.explanation: Laysa is a sister of kana, so its predicate must be in the accusative case (مُفيداً).

tip: Remember: Kana 'steals' the damma from the predicate and turns it into fatha, while keeping the subject nominative.

title: Inna and Its Sisters (Inna wa Akhawatuha)
subtitle: Adding emphasis and nuance by placing the subject into the accusative case
keyPoint: Inna and its sisters govern nominal sentences by putting the subject into the accusative (Mansub) while leaving the predicate nominative (Marfu').

examples.en: إِنَّ الطّالِبَيْنِ مُتَفَوِّقانِ في اللُّغَةِ العَرَبِيَّةِ.

mistakes.note: The noun directly following Inna is its subject (Ism Inna) and must take the accusative case (fatha).
After the verb qala (قالَ), you must always use Inna (إِنَّ) with a kasra, never Anna (أَنَّ).
Masculine plural nouns following Inna become accusative, changing the suffix from -oona to -eena.

quiz.question: Choose the correct voweling: 'إِنَّ ___ جَميلٌ.' (Indeed, the view is beautiful)
quiz.explanation: The noun following 'Inna' is in the accusative (Mansub), requiring a fatha (المَنْظَرَ).

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'قالَ أَبي: ___ الصِّدْقَ فَضيلَةٌ.' (My father said: Indeed, truthfulness is a virtue)
quiz.explanation: After forms of the verb قالَ (to say), 'إِنَّ' is required rather than 'أَنَّ'.

quiz.question: Identify the correct form: 'عَرَفْتُ أَنَّ ___ قادِمونَ.' (I learned that the guests are coming)
quiz.explanation: The subject of 'Anna' takes the accusative case (fatha: الضُّيوفَ).

quiz.question: Select the correct combination: 'لَعَلَّ المُسافِرَ ___.' (Perhaps the traveler returns/is returning)
quiz.explanation: The predicate of La'alla remains in the nominative case (Marfu') with tanwin damma (عائِدٌ).

tip: Contrast trick: Kana makes the predicate accusative; Inna makes the subject accusative. They are exact grammatical mirrors!

title: Weak, Assimilated, and Defective Verbs (Al-Mu'tall)
subtitle: Navigating roots with Waw and Ya through vowel mutations, drops, and shortenings
keyPoint: Weak radicals (و or ي) mutate into long vowels, shorten before sukūn, or disappear entirely across conjugations.

cells: Initial Waw drops in present tense
Weak letter becomes alif/ya depending on suffix

examples.en: نَسِيَ أَخي مَفاتيحَ البَيْتِ في الدَّاخِلِ.

mistakes.note: Hollow verbs drop their long vowel when conjugated with consonant subject suffixes (e.g. tu, ta, na) because two consonants cannot carry sukun consecutively.
The initial Waw in Form I assimilated verbs (Mithal) regularly drops in the present tense (يَصِلُ, not يَوْصِلُ).
In the jussive mood after 'lam' (لَمْ), defective verbs drop their final weak vowel completely.

quiz.question: Conjugate 'زارَ' (to visit) for 'I' in the past: 'أَنا ___ صَديقي.'
quiz.explanation: Because the middle vowel in the present is 'u' (يَزورُ), the past stem shortens to damma before 'tu': زُرْتُ.

quiz.question: What is the present tense of 'وَجَدَ' (to find) for 'he'?
quiz.explanation: In Form I assimilated verbs, the initial Waw drops in the present tense, yielding يَجِدُ.

quiz.question: Conjugate with the jussive negative particle: 'لَمْ ___ عَلَى السُّؤالِ.' (He did not respond from دَعا/يَدْعو)
quiz.explanation: The jussive mood of a defective verb shortens the final long vowel to a short damma: لَمْ يَدْعُ.

quiz.question: Conjugate 'رَمى' (to throw) for 'they (masc. pl.)' in the past: 'هُمْ ___ الكُرَةَ.'
quiz.explanation: With the masculine plural 'waw al-jama'a', final alif maqsura opens to an -aw diphthong: رَمَوْا.

tip: To determine the short vowel of a hollow verb in the past (قُلْتُ vs. بِعْتُ), look at its present-tense vowel: يَقولُ gives 'u' (قُلْتُ), while يَبيعُ gives 'i' (بِعْتُ).

title: The Circumstantial Accusative (Al-Hal)
subtitle: Depicting simultaneous physical states and manner using accusative words or clauses
keyPoint: A Hal must be indefinite and accusative (Mansub) while its referent (Sahib al-Hal) is definite, answering the question 'How?'.

cells: Introduced by Waw al-Hal + independent sentence
Imperfect verb directly functioning as simultaneous state

mistakes.note: If you make the participle definite with 'al-', it becomes an adjective (The smiling student came), not a circumstantial Hal (The student came smiling).
Defective active participles restore their ya and take tanwin fatha in the accusative Hal form.
In a Hal clause following Waw al-Hal, the clause is an independent equational sentence where subject and predicate remain nominative.

quiz.question: Select the correct Hal form: 'رَجَعَ الجُنودُ مِنَ المَعْرَكَةِ ___.' (The soldiers returned victorious)
quiz.explanation: The Hal must be accusative. For sound masculine plural, the accusative suffix is -ina: مُنْتَصِرينَ.

quiz.question: Turn into a proper Hal: 'جَلَسْتُ في الغُرْفَةِ ___ الكِتابَ.' (I sat in the room reading the book)
quiz.explanation: An imperfect (present) verb clause can function directly as a Hal depicting an ongoing action simultaneous with the main verb.

quiz.question: Choose the correct Waw al-Hal structure: 'وَصَلَ الطُّلّابُ ___.' (The students arrived while the teacher was absent)
quiz.explanation: After Waw al-Hal, a nominal clause is composed of normal nominative mubtada' and khabar: والمُعَلِّمُ غائِبٌ.

quiz.question: Identify the Hal in: 'أَكَلَ أَخي الطَّعامَ واقِفاً.' (My brother ate the food standing)
quiz.explanation: 'واقِفاً' is an indefinite accusative active participle that explains the physical state of the brother during the eating.

tip: Check test: Ask 'كَيْفَ؟' (How?). If your word answers how the subject or object was behaving at the exact moment the verb occurred, it is a Hal!

title: Diptotes (Al-Mamnu' min Al-Sarf)
subtitle: Special nouns and adjectives barred from nunation and taking fatha in the genitive
keyPoint: Diptotes cannot receive nunation (tanwīn) and take a fatḥa instead of a kasra when in the genitive case, unless prefixed by 'al-' or annexed in an Iḍāfa.

cells: Reverts to normal kasra when made definite

examples.en: قَرَأْتُ عَنْ عُلَماءَ عَباقِرَةٍ في التَّاريخِ.

mistakes.note: Foreign/feminine city names are diptotes; they never take tanwin and take fatha in the genitive after prepositions.
Proper names on the pattern of فُعَل (Fu'al) such as 'Umar are diptotes and take fatha in the genitive without nunation.
When a diptote receives the definite article 'al-' (الـ), its diptote status is disabled and it takes a normal kasra.

quiz.question: Choose the correctly vowelled diptote: 'سَلَّمْتُ عَلَى ___.' (I greeted Ibrahim)
quiz.explanation: Foreign proper names are diptotic: in the genitive position after 'عَلَى', they take a fatha without tanwin (إِبْراهيمَ).

quiz.question: Select the correct form: 'اشْتَرَيْتُ سَيّارَةً ذاتَ لَوْنٍ ___.' (I bought a car of a green color)
quiz.explanation: Color adjectives matching the pattern أَفْعَل are diptotes and take fatha in the genitive (أَخْضَرَ).

quiz.question: What happens when 'مَساجِد' has 'al-': 'اعْتَكَفَ الرَّجُلُ في ___.' (The man retreated in the mosques)
quiz.explanation: The moment a diptote is made definite by 'al-' (الـ), it returns to normal triptote declension and takes a standard kasra (المَساجِدِ).

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT a diptote?
quiz.explanation: The name 'مُحَمَّد' is fully declinable (Triptote / Masruf) and accepts tanwin (مُحَمَّدٌ, مُحَمَّداً, مُحَمَّدٍ).

tip: Two keys break the diptote shield: add 'الـ' to the front OR put it first in an Idafa chain, and it instantly behaves like a normal noun with kasra!
